body.p: The Office Action dated August 1, 2023, is received and carefully noted. Claims 1 and 7-9 are amended. Claims 2-5 are cancelled, without prejudice. Support for the amendments may be found in the cancelled claims. Claims 1 and 6-9 are pending in the present application and
respectfully submitted for reconsideration in view of the foregoing amendments and the following remarks.

Applicants acknowledge with appreciation the courtesy provided to Applicants' representative during the interviews with Examiner Lodge and Examiner Porter on October 16, 2023, and November 1, 2023. The feedback provided by Examiners Lodge and Porter helped to further prosecution of the present application.

Figure 1 is objected to for informalities. Applicants submit a replacement Figure 1 to correct the informalities. Specifically, the text in elements 2 and 13 are redone to form complete words. Applicants submit that the objection is rendered moot. Withdrawal of the objection to Figure 1 is respectfully requested.

Claim 5 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as allegedly being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter of the invention. Claim 5 is cancelled, without prejudice, by the foregoing amendments. Thus, the rejection of claim 5 is rendered moot. Withdrawal of the indefiniteness rejection is respectfully requested.

Claims 1-9 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as allegedly being directed to an abstract idea. Specifically, the Office Action alleges that the claims are directed to a mathematical concept and a mental process. Applicants extensively amend the independent claims to recite patent-eligible
subject matter. Applicants submit that claims 1, 8, and 9 do not recite a mathematical concept or a mental process.

For example, claims 1, 8, and 9 now recite collecting RRI data over at least a two hour time period, which would generate about 7200 pieces of data, or 60 pieces of data per minute. Further, the feature vector is generated instantaneously from the large amounts of data provided by the heart rate measuring instrument including the steps of comparing each piece of data to a threshold and forming the feature based on the comparison before input into the recurrent neural network. Applicants submit that these actions may not be performed mentally by human or just applying a mathematical concept. The limitations recited in claims 1, 8, and 9 cannot practically be performed in the human mind.

Applicants also submit that claims 1, 8, and 9 recite a practical application of any potential abstract idea. As noted in paragraph [0030] of the published application and shown in Figures 7A- 1 IB, the determination accuracy of whether a subject has sleep apnea is significantly improved. Use of the Long Short-Term Memory neural network further improves this accuracy. Referring to paragraph [0033], improvement in the accuracy of determining sleep apnea also may be found in using a variable length feature vector as opposed to a fixed length. The claims also recite limitations that remove some of the RRI data from the feature vector for a specified interval. All of these features improve accuracy of the model, as shown in Figure 12 of the present application. Thus, the

claims also recite a practical application of any potential abstract ideas.For these reasons, Applicants submit that claims 1, 8, and 9, as amended, recite patent- eligible subject matter. Applicants respectfully request that the rejection under Section 101 be withdrawn.
Claims 1-2, 4, and 6-9 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as allegedly being unpatentable

over Fujiwara (Japanese Patent Publication No. 2016-214491) in view of Mitsukura (WIPO Publication No. 2018221750 and Sakamoto (WIPO Publication No. 2009150765). Claim 3 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Fujiwara in view of Mitsukura and Sakamoto, and further in view of Kogure (WIPO Publication No. 2019107012). Claim 5 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Fujiwara in view of Mitsukura and Sakamoto, and further in view of Liu (Chinese Patent Publication No. 109117730). With regard to claim 5, as this claim is cancelled, Applicants submit this rejection is rendered moot. Applicants respectfully traverse the remaining rejections. The cited references, either alone or in combination, fail to disclose or suggest the limitations of the pending claims.

Claims 1, 8, and 9 are the independent claims. Claim 1 recites "instantaneously generating a feature vector including a plurality of heart rate intervals that are consecutive in the sleeping period, wherein the feature vector is a variable length vector formed as a time series of a group of pieces of the normal RRI data having normal values respectively indicating the plurality of heart rate intervals in an identification target period having a fixed period length of about 60 seconds." Claim 1 also recites "inputting the variable length vector formed as the time series of the group of pieces of the normal RRI data as the feature vector to the processing unit operating as a recurrent neural network trained through machine learning in advance so as to output, in response to the feature vector having been inputted, a value indicating a sleep state in the identification target period." Claims 8 and 9 recite similar limitations. Applicants submit that the cited references fail to disclose or suggest these limitations of claims 1, 8, and 9.

Fujiwara is the primary reference. The Office Action concedes that Fujiwara "does not teach wherein the identification target period has a fixed period length, and the feature vector is a variable length vector formed as a time series of a group of pieces of RRI data respectively indicating the plurality of heart rate intervals in the identification target period," on page 11, under the section discussing cancelled claim 4. The Office Action, however, cites Mitsukura as teaching these features of amended claims 1, 8, and 9.

Reference is made to U.S. Patent Publication No. 2021/0137452, which is the counterpart U.S. application to Mitsukura, also referred to as Mitsukura below. Referring to paragraphs [0070]- [0072] in the copending U.S. Publication, Mitsukura describes inputting heart rate feature values, or heart rate variability parameters (HRV parameters), into the neural network. Variable extraction unit 102a in sleep determination apparatus 100 extracts HRV parameters from the heart rate variability data stored in the storage unit 106. HRV parameters include the very low frequency (VLF) component, a ratio of a low frequency (LF) component to a high frequency (HF) component, a mean heartbeat interval (RRI), and a standard deviation of each heartbeat interval (RRI) of the heart rate.

Applicants submit that the HRV parameters do not disclose or suggest a variable length vector formed as a time series of a group of pieces of the normal RRI data having normal values. In Mitsukura, RRI data itself is not inputted into the neural network. Further, each piece of RRI is not used to generate the feature vector as a variable length vector. As stated in paragraphs [0044]-[0046] of Mitsukura and paragraphs [0070]-[0072] of the publication of the U.S. copending application:

Referring back to FIG. 2, subsequently, the control unit 102 of the sleep determination apparatus 100 stores the heart rate signal data input from the input unit 112 in the storage unit 106 (step SB-2). The storage unit 106 may store the heart rate signal data in advance, or the sleep determination apparatus 100 may receive the heart rate signal data stored in the external device 200 and store the heart rate signal
data in the storage unit 106.

Then, the variable extraction unit 102a in the sleep determination apparatus 100 extracts heart rate variability parameters to be used for the determination technique set in step SB-1 from the heart rate variability data stored in the storage unit 106 (step SB-2). For example, the variable extraction unit 102amay extract the VLF, the LF, the HF, the mean RRI, the standard deviation of each RRI, the LF/HF ratio, and so on
by using a known heart rate variability parameter extraction technique.
Then, the sleep stage determination unit 102b in the sleep determination apparatus

100 determines a sleep stage using, as inputs, the heart rate variability parameters extracted by the variable extraction unit 102a, in accordance with the determination technique set in step SB-1 (step SB-4). As an example, the sleep stage determination unit 102b may determine light sleep among the sleep stages using one-vs-rest
classification.

Applicants submit that the HRV parameters of Mitsukura do not disclose or suggest "a variable length vector formed as a time series of a group of pieces of the normal RRI data having normal values respectively indicating the plurality of heart rate intervals in an identification target period having a fixed period length of about 60 seconds," as recited in claims 1, 8, and 9. There is a distinction between the RRI data recited in the claims and the HRV parameters taught by Mitsukura. As noted in paragraph [0041] of the present specification:

As another example of the feature vector, a vector composed of a plurality of HRV indexes is also conceivable. The HRV indexes can be two or more indexes among (1) to (11) below, for example. As an example, identification of the sleep state using the HRV index is performed in a determination technique in which: whether the subject has apnea or normal respiration is identified for each time period during sleep; and temporal variation indicating whether the subject has apnea or normal respiration is obtained. This determination technique uses, as an example of an identification model, a support vector machine that discriminates between an apnea
state and a normal respiration state when given an HRV index.
Thus, the HRV index differs from the RRI data within the feature vector recited in the claims. As stated in paragraph [0042] of the present specification:
Here, each RRI is a value directly obtained from an electrocardiographic waveform of the subject, and consecutive RRIs can be said to be a value group directly

representing the feature of the electrocardiographic waveform in the sleeping period of the subject. The inventors analyzed that since each HRV index is an index calculated from RRIs and a value relevant to RRIs, the HRV index does not provide direct representation when compared with RRIs. Therefore, based on this analysis, the inventors decided to generate a feature vector from RRIs themselves, and to use the generated feature vector in the identification process described later.

Accordingly, a more direct feature of the electrocardiographic waveform than when a feature vector generated from the HRV indexes is used will be used in the identification process described later. As a result, the determination accuracy can be
improved.

For these reasons, Applicants submit that the HRV parameters of Mitsukura fail to disclose or suggest the feature vector being a variable length vector, as recited in the independent claims. Applicants submit that Mitsukura fails to disclose or suggest the limitations of claims 1, 8, and 9 missing from Fujiwara.

Applicants also submit that Sakamoto fails to disclose or suggest the limitations of claims 1, 8, and 9 missing from Fujiwara and Mitsukura. The Office Action does not apply Sakamoto against the claims as teaching the limitations of claims 1, 8, and 9 discussed above. Instead, the Office Action cites Sakamoto as teaching "being obtained for each identification target period." Sakamoto describes calculating a power spectrum and LF/HF parameters to form RRI data, as shown in Figures 4 and 6. Sakamoto fails to disclose or suggest the recurrent neural network is configured to be inputted with the variable length vector formed as a time series of a group of pieces of the normal RRI data. Thus, Applicants submit that Sakamoto cannot be held to disclose or suggest the limitations of claims 1, 8, and 9 missing from Fujiwara and Mitsukura.
With regard to the secondary references of Kogure and Liu, Applicants respectfully submit that these references fail to disclose or suggest the limitations of claims 1, 8, and 9 missing from
Fujiwara, Mitsukura, and Sakamoto. Further, the Office Action does not apply Kogure or Liu against claims 1, 8, and 9.

For at least these reasons, claims 1, 8, and 9 are not rendered obvious by the cited references, either alone or in combination. The remaining claims depend from claim 1. Applicants submit that the dependent claims also distinguish over the cited references for the reasons provided above. Based on these patentable distinctions, Applicants respectfully request that the obviousness rejections be withdrawn.

The claims of the application are accordingly submitted to be in condition for allowance, and passage to issue is respectfully requested. However, should the Examiner have any questions or comments which would expedite prosecution, he/she is cordially invited to telephone the undersigned at the number below.
